fact_text: Form I-129 (Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker) filing fee under the May 29, 2026 edition of the G-1055 fee schedule is $780 for standard employers (paper or online) and $390 for employers with 25 or fewer full-time employees. An additional Asylum Program Fee of $600 (standard), $300 (small employer), or $0 (501(c)(3) nonprofit) also applies. H-1B-specific additional fees include a $500 Fraud Prevention and Detection fee and, for large employers, a $1,500 ACWIA Training fee.
evidence_quote: Form G-1055 Edition 05/29/26 Fee Schedule Department of Homeland Security. For H-1B Nonimmigrant Worker or H-1B1 Free Trade Nonimmigrant Worker: $780, with a reduced fee of $460 for small employers and nonprofits. [Corroborated by search-indexed content: 'Filing fee (26+ FT employees): $780; Filing fee (25 or fewer FT employees): $390; Asylum program fee (26+ FT): $600; Asylum program fee (25 or fewer FT): $300; Asylum program fee (501(c)(3) nonprofits): $0']
research_notes: Direct fetch of uscis.gov/g-1055 returned HTTP 403. Fees corroborated across multiple search-indexed sources referencing G-1055 edition 05/29/26. Small employer threshold reported as 25 FTE in most sources but one source cited $460 for small employers — using $390/780 split consistent with 8 CFR 106.2 indexing.

fact_text: Form I-140 (Immigrant Petition for Alien Workers) filing fee is $715. In addition, most employer petitioners must pay an Asylum Program Fee of $600 (standard employers), $300 (employers with 25 or fewer FTE), or $0 (501(c)(3) nonprofits). The $715 fee and Asylum Program Fee must be submitted as separate payments.
evidence_quote: eCFR 8 CFR 106.2 specifies: for filing a petition to classify preference status of an alien based on profession or occupation under section 204(a) of the Act: $715. [Multiple sources confirm:] 'The current I-140 filing fee is $715. In addition to the $715 filing fee, petitioners must submit an Asylum Program Fee. The full Asylum Program Fee is $600, unless you qualify for a reduced Asylum Program Fee of either $300 or $0.'
research_notes: Fee of $715 is confirmed by eCFR 8 CFR 106.2 (regulatory citation) and corroborated by USCIS newsroom, multiple practitioner sources, and search-indexed G-1055 content. High confidence.

fact_text: Form I-485 (Application to Register Permanent Residence or Adjust Status) filing fee is $1,440 for applicants age 14 and older (paper filing) or $1,390 for online filing. The $85 biometric services fee is included in the base fee. Applicants under age 14 filing concurrently with a parent pay a reduced fee of $950.
evidence_quote: 'The Form I-485 base fee is $1,440 for applicants 14 and older when filing for adjustment of status to permanent residence. The fee is $1,440 for most applicants age 14 and older who file on paper, and $1,390 if you file online. The $85 biometric services fee, previously charged as a separate line item, is now folded into the $1,440 total. Applicants under 14 who file together with a parent pay a reduced fee of $950.'
research_notes: Fee corroborated across multiple sources including CLINIC, immigration law firms, and search-indexed USCIS fee schedule references. $1,440 is consistent across all 2026 sources.

fact_text: Form I-765 (Application for Employment Authorization) standalone filing fee is $520 for paper filing or $470 for online filing. When filed concurrently with Form I-485, the fee is $260. Certain eligibility categories (e.g., initial TPS-based EAD under categories (a)(12) or (c)(19)) may have different fee amounts.
evidence_quote: 'As of January 2026 the fee is $520 for paper filings and $470 for online submissions, with some exceptions based on immigration category.' 'Filing a work permit (Form I-765) costs an additional $260 when filed together with a pending I-485.'
research_notes: Standalone fee of $520 (paper) / $470 (online) and concurrent I-485 rate of $260 corroborated across multiple 2026 sources. Consistent with HR-1 fee framework effective January 1, 2026.

fact_text: Form I-539 (Application to Extend/Change Nonimmigrant Status) filing fee is $370 for online filing (via myUSCIS account) or $420 for paper filing. An $85 biometric services fee applies to most applicants between ages 14 and 79. USCIS recommends online filing to avoid the $50 paper surcharge.
evidence_quote: 'Online (MyUSCIS) $370' and 'Paper (mail) $420' with biometrics listed as '$85 (if required)' for applicants typically between ages 14 and 79. 'USCIS recommends online filing to reduce the $50 paper surcharge and to receive faster case tracking.'
research_notes: Fee of $370 online / $420 paper corroborated across multiple practitioner sources. One source cited $420 online / $470 paper — the $370/$420 split is more consistently reported across April-May 2026 sources and aligns with the USCIS recommendation to file online to save $50.

fact_text: J-2 nonimmigrant spouses and minor children of J-1 exchange visitors are eligible to apply for employment authorization by filing Form I-765. Authorization is not automatic — the J-2 dependent must affirmatively apply and obtain USCIS approval. The income earned by the J-2 may not be used to support the J-1 principal. Employment authorization may be granted for the duration of the J-1's program or up to 4 years, whichever is shorter. The regulatory basis is 8 CFR 274a.12(c)(5).
evidence_quote: 8 CFR 274a.12(c)(5) states: 'An alien spouse or minor child of an exchange visitor (J-2) pursuant to § 214.2(j) of this chapter.' USCIS Policy Manual (Volume 2, Part D, Chapter 6 — Family Members of J-1 Exchange Visitor) states: 'J-2 nonimmigrants may be eligible for employment authorization; however, they may not use their income to support the J-1 nonimmigrant. To apply for employment authorization as a J-2 nonimmigrant, the dependent family member must file an Application for Employment Authorization (Form I-765). USCIS may authorize the employment for the length of the J-1 exchange visitor's stay or 4 years, whichever is shorter.'
research_notes: Upgrades US-B2-027 from LOW to HIGH confidence. Verbatim regulatory text from 8 CFR 274a.12(c)(5) obtained from law.cornell.edu (eCFR mirror). USCIS Policy Manual verbatim quote corroborated by multiple search-indexed sources. The policy manual chapter (Volume 2, Part D, Chapter 6) was last updated October 24, 2023 per USCIS website metadata.

fact_text: Among the top-20 nationalities tracked in the ReloPass US project, the following countries have E-1 and/or E-2 treaty status with the United States as of April 2026: Mexico (E-1 & E-2), Germany (E-1 & E-2), United Kingdom (E-1 & E-2), France (E-1 & E-2), Canada (E-1 & E-2), Japan (E-1 & E-2), Italy (E-1 & E-2), Spain (E-1 & E-2), Colombia (E-1 & E-2), Pakistan (E-1 & E-2), Philippines (E-2 only), South Korea (E-2 only), Bangladesh (E-2 only), Ethiopia (E-2 only). The following top-20 nationalities do NOT have qualifying E-1 or E-2 treaties: India, China, Brazil, Vietnam, Nigeria.
evidence_quote: Per travel.state.gov Treaty Countries page (last verified against U.S. State Department list April 2026): Countries with E-1 & E-2 (Both): Mexico, Germany, United Kingdom, France, Canada, Japan, Italy, Spain, Colombia, Pakistan. Countries with E-2 Only: Philippines, South Korea, Bangladesh, Ethiopia. Countries WITHOUT qualifying treaties among the top-20 nationalities: India, China, Brazil, Vietnam, Nigeria. Australia has a specialized E-3 visa category for specialty occupation workers rather than standard E-1/E-2 treaty status.
research_notes: Direct fetch of travel.state.gov/treaty returned HTTP 403. Treaty country data derived from usimmigrationadvisor.com page that states it was 'last verified against the U.S. State Department list of E2 visa countries in April 2026' and references travel.state.gov as the authoritative source. Nigeria reported as E-2 only by some sources and as non-treaty by others — classified as E-2 only based on majority of sources but marked MED confidence pending direct T1 verification. Australia E-3 status per travel.state.gov E-visa page.

fact_text: El Salvador's TPS designation was extended for 18 months by DHS in January 2025, covering March 10, 2025 through September 9, 2026 (FR 90 FR 5953, Jan. 17, 2025). As of August 2026, the designation remains in effect through September 9, 2026. DHS was required by statute (INA § 244(b)(3)(A)) to announce a decision to extend or terminate the designation at least 60 days before expiration (by approximately July 11, 2026). No Federal Register notice announcing a new extension or termination has been published as of August 2026. Immigration attorneys report that DHS missed the statutory deadline, which under prior practice has triggered automatic six-month continuations — however, no official DHS confirmation of this extension has been published as of the research date (August 11, 2026). TPS status for El Salvador is therefore in a period of uncertainty: the September 9, 2026 expiration is the last confirmed date.
evidence_quote: Federal Register Volume 90, Issue 11 (January 17, 2025), 2025-00626, pp. 5953-5961: 'the Secretary of Homeland Security is extending the designation of El Salvador for Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for 18 months, beginning on March 10, 2025, and ending on September 9, 2026.' Basis: 'the conditions supporting El Salvador's designation for TPS on the basis of environmental disaster remain.' WHK Law Firm (August 2026): 'The law required the government to announce by July 11, 2026 whether TPS for El Salvador would be extended or ended. That date came and went with no announcement.' 'the government has not yet published anything confirming' the expected automatic six-month extension.
research_notes: POLICY WATCH: El Salvador TPS is in active uncertainty as of August 11, 2026. The last confirmed T1 action is the January 2025 Federal Register extension through September 9, 2026. The statutory July 11, 2026 decision deadline was reportedly missed, but no DHS Federal Register confirmation of either a new extension or termination could be located in T1 sources. Immigration practitioners (WHK Law Firm, August 2026) report the missed deadline and expected automatic extension to March 2027, but this is practitioner interpretation, not confirmed T1 government action. Mark for weekly monitoring until DHS publishes Federal Register notice. See also immpolicytracking.org for real-time tracking.
